summary: Waterborne 45 nm polymethyl methacrylate nanoplastics altered lipid metabolism genes and raised oxidative status and blood cell genotoxicity in gilthead seabream.
Microplastics suppressed immune and neural biomarkers in blood clams and aggravated the immunotoxic and neurotoxic effects of bisphenol A.
Ninety days of 0.5 micrometre polystyrene microplastics raised troponin I and caused cardiac fibrosis and cardiomyocyte apoptosis through Wnt and beta-catenin signalling in rats.
Eluates of low-degraded plastics were more toxic to nematode lifespan, DNA integrity and germline apoptosis than those of highly degraded fragments.
Positively charged polystyrene nanoparticles accumulated more in human alveolar cells under cyclic stretch and activated apoptotic signalling.
A microFTIR method was developed to extract and quantify microplastics under 100 micrometres in Pacific oysters; a method paper.
Four size classes of polyethylene microplastics in sediment produced no adverse biochemical, physiological or reproductive effects in blackworms.
Heating element compositions and temperatures characterised in vaping cartridges linked to lung injury; a device materials study.
Review of the stress and immunity axis in shellfish across environmental perturbations; aquaculture health, not plastic particles specifically.
Polystyrene microplastics of 5 micrometres lowered epididymal sperm viability and raised testicular NF-kB, IL-1beta and IL-6 in mice.
Acute maternal pulmonary exposure to nanopolystyrene in late pregnancy translocated particles to rat placental and fetal tissues with adverse fetoplacental effects.
Polystyrene nanoplastics accumulated in primary mouse brain cells, with reactive astrocytosis contributing to apoptosis of defective neurons.
Thirty days of dietary polyethylene microplastics altered blood biochemical parameters and lowered triglycerides in European pond turtles.
Polyethylene microbeads proved more toxic to medaka eyes and reproduction than to kidneys or growth, with oxidative stress and defined effect levels.
A modified OECD 412 whole-body inhalation study in rats found polystyrene micro and nanoplastics affected the lung at molecular rather than organismal level.
Polystyrene microplastics produced proinflammatory and lipid changes in the livers of mice with acute colitis, apparently through raised intestinal permeability.
Review of microbes and enzymes that degrade synthetic plastics; biodegradation chemistry with no health endpoint.
Nanoplastics drove oxidative stress in marine medaka while microplastics drove gut dysbiosis with immune dysfunction, indicating distinct size-dependent pathways.
In a triple-culture human intestinal model, PVC particles raised IL-1beta release and caused epithelial cell loss only in the inflamed condition.
Transcriptome sequencing of Daphnia pulex neonates found 208 genes changed by nanoplastic exposure across oxidative stress, immune defence and glycometabolism.
Polystyrene microplastics caused hepatic inflammation, apoptosis and oxidative stress in mice, which hydrogen sulfide mitigated through Keap1 and Nrf2 signalling.
Polystyrene microplastics transformed by simulated gastric fluid became more cytotoxic to liver cells, raising apoptosis through oxidative stress.
Microplastic fibres caused length-dependent intestinal damage in zebrafish, with longer fibres cutting food intake and disturbing lipid metabolism.
Polystyrene microplastics raised phenanthrene accumulation in zebrafish and the combination exacerbated antioxidant, immune and gut microflora changes.
Twenty-one days of waterborne polystyrene microplastics produced molecular and histological alterations in zebrafish gonads at the higher concentration.
